name: CryptOpt
baseline: GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6 compiling Fiat Cryptography's generated C at -O3 -march=native -mtune=native; also hand-optimized assembly (OpenSSL fe-51/fe-64, libsecp256k1 asm, HACL* fe-64)
metric: latency (CPU cycles per finite-field multiply and square)
workload: Multiply and square in nine prime fields (Curve25519, NIST P-224/P-256/P-384/P-521, secp256k1, Curve448, SIKEp434 field, Poly1305) on ten x86-64 CPUs, plus scalar multiplication through SUPERCOP.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: mean speedup 1.74 over GCC 12.1.0 and 1.40 over Clang 15.0.6 across ten x86-64 platforms; 1.04 average speedup over the hand-optimized assembly in libsecp256k1. Table 4 geometric means of CryptOpt over Clang / GCC, Mul: Curve25519 1.25/1.16, P-224 1.54/2.52, P-256 1.70/2.61, P-384 1.45/2.49, SIKEp434 1.70/2.43, Curve448 1.19/0.98, P-521 1.30/0.97, Poly1305 1.12/1.22, secp256k1 1.80/2.62.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline C built with GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6, highest optimization level with -march=native -mtune=native -O3; CPU frequency fixed, boosting disabled, performance governor; Ubuntu Server 22.04.1.
hardware: Ten x86-64 machines: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1900X (Zen 1), Ryzen 7 5800X and Ryzen 9 5950X (Zen 3), Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4); Intel Core i7-6770HQ, i7-10710U, i9-10900K, i7-11700KF, i9-12900KF, i9-13900KF (performance cores only).
stars_or_usage: 73 stars; PLDI 2023 distinguished paper; verified assembly published in the fiat-crypto fiat-amd64 directory
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; the assembly is found by randomized search per microarchitecture (20 to 40 wall-clock hours per machine for the 18 primitives) and must be regenerated for new CPUs; correctness is checked by an equivalence checker only when the input is Fiat IR, the libsecp256k1 variant is unverified; fixed-size field arithmetic, not a general library.
caveats: The assembly is machine-generated, not hand-written (it is placed here because it is compared against both compilers and hand-written assembly). Gains vary: Curve448 and P-521 multiply are slightly slower than GCC (0.98 and 0.97); gains are modest for Curve25519 and Poly1305. The baseline is Fiat's generated C, not each library's own C. In whole-scalar-multiplication tests (Table 5) CryptOpt-enhanced code is on par with OpenSSL fe-51/fe-64 asm and below HACL* fe-64 asm. The artifact lives on Zenodo (not opened); the repo README repeats the Table 4 means. Last commit is almost three years old.
found_via: WebSearch 'CryptOpt verified compilation randomized program search assembly faster than gcc clang -O3'; PLDI 2023 paper PDF read from the repo's papers/ directory via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: pqm4
baseline: PQClean 'clean' portable C implementations of ML-KEM and ML-DSA built with the same arm-none-eabi-gcc at -O3
workload: ML-KEM-512/768/1024 KeyGen, Encaps, Decaps and ML-DSA-44/65/87 KeyGen, Sign, Verify on a Cortex-M4 board at 24 MHz: Cortex-M4(F)-specific implementations (m4f, m4fspeed, typically assembly) versus clean C.
claimed_speedup: Cycle counts from benchmarks.md (ratios derived from page data). ml-kem-768 KeyGen/Encaps/Decaps: clean 988,722 / 1,138,225 / 1,387,984 vs m4fspeed 642,096 / 658,754 / 707,827 (1.54x / 1.73x / 1.96x). ml-kem-512 KeyGen 595,793 vs 392,423; Decaps 888,653 vs 428,167 (2.08x). ml-dsa-44 KeyGen/Sign/Verify: clean 1,874,405 / 7,925,955 / 2,063,096 vs m4f 1,426,025 / 3,943,121 / 1,421,623 (1.31x / 2.01x / 1.45x).
compiler_and_flags: arm-none-eabi-gcc (Arm GNU Toolchain 11.3.Rel1) 11.3.1 20220712; default --opt speed, which the mupq build system maps to -O3 -g3
hardware: NUCLEO-L4R5ZI (STM32L4R5, Cortex-M4F) at 24 MHz to avoid flash wait states; min/max/avg over 100 executions (fewer for slow schemes)
stars_or_usage: 456 stars, 124 forks; de-facto PQC benchmark framework for Cortex-M4
tradeoffs: Cortex-M4/M4F specific (ARMv7E-M assembly, FPU registers in m4f); not portable to other cores. m4fspeed ML-KEM-768 code size is 16,016 bytes vs 5,120 for clean in the size table; the m4fstack variants trade speed for stack. Each implementation directory carries its own LICENSE.
caveats: The m4/m4f implementations are 'typically' assembly, some are mixed C and assembly, so the comparison is optimized-M4 vs portable C rather than strictly hand-asm vs C. SPHINCS+ rows have only a clean C implementation. The README now carries a deprecation notice: the project is no longer under active maintenance and is likely to be archived in or after January 2027. Same compiler for both sides; hash and NTT share of time differs by variant.
found_via: github.com repo pages for Cortex-M4 post-quantum assembly after the Neon NTT paper search; benchmarks.md and mupq/mk/config.mk read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: PQRV (Keccak, Kyber, Dilithium on RV{32,64}IM{B}{V})
baseline: pq-crystals reference C for Kyber (ref, commit 441c051) and Dilithium (ref, commit f1f8085) and PQClean fips202.c for Keccak (commit 05df469), compiled with the XuanTie GCC 10.4.0 at -O3 on the same core
workload: Keccak-f1600/SHAKE, Kyber768 KeyGen/Encaps/Decaps and Dilithium3 KeyGen/Sign/Verify on a XuanTie C908 core, RV32/RV64 with and without B (bit-manip) and V (vector) extensions.
claimed_speedup: Table 4 (k cycles, derived ratios from page data): Kyber768 KeyGen ref RV64IM 742k vs ours RV64IM 278k and RV64IMBV 165k (4.5x); ref RV32IM 1222k vs ours RV32IM 496k and RV32IMBV 284k. Dilithium3 Sign ref RV64IM 8232k vs ours RV64IMBV 2139k; ref RV32IM 13671k vs ours RV32IMBV 3054k. Text: Keccak RV64I 90% faster and RV32I twice as fast as the C reference; 'speedups of nearly 2x or more' for Kyber/Dilithium over the C reference.
compiler_and_flags: Xuantie-900 linux-5.10.4 glibc GCC toolchain V2.8.0 (GCC 10.4.0), all programs compiled with -O3 and -static; Makefiles and result .txt files in the repo (ches2025 branch reproduces the paper)
hardware: CanMV-K230 board, XuanTie C908 core (RV{32,64}GCBV, VLEN=128, 1.6 GHz, dual-issue in-order); repo also supports SpacemiT X60 (VLEN=256)
stars_or_usage: 15 stars; artifact of a TCHES 2025 paper
tradeoffs: Hand-written assembly per ISA variant (the sha3 directory alone has 49 .S files); tuned for dual-issue in-order RISC-V cores (C908, X60) and specific extensions B and V; RVV code assumes VLEN of 128 or 256; not portable and not a drop-in library API (derived from pq-crystals code). Constant-time claims are the authors'.
caveats: Reference C numbers depend on the compiler exploiting B-extension rotates (the paper's RV64IB Keccak assembly is only 36% faster than the C reference, versus 90% on RV64I, because the compiler uses rotate and andn). Paper comparisons with Cortex-A72 NEON and Cortex-M4 are labelled 'unfair, for reference only'. The repo's main branch has been updated beyond the paper (FIPS 203 changes); reproduce from the ches2025 branch. Medians over 10000 iterations except Dilithium Sign (average). The paper PDF was read through a raw.githubusercontent.com mirror of the author's site.
found_via: github.com/Ji-Peng repo pages seen while searching PQC assembly artifacts; paper PDF fetched from the author's Ji-Peng.github.io repository via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: memcpy_benchmark (AVX-256, AVX-512 and rep movsb NASM memcpy)
baseline: libc built-in memcpy (glibc version not stated)
workload: Multithreaded memory-copy benchmark running the libc memcpy against NASM AVX-256, AVX-512 and rep movsb memcpy routines; Max/Min/Avg/Total over repeated runs.
claimed_speedup: result.txt (unit not stated, lower is better; ratios derived from page data). Xeon Platinum 8269CY: libc memcpy avg 0.3853 vs AVX-256 asm avg 0.2987 (about 1.29x) and AVX-512 asm avg 0.3150. AMD A8-6410: libc avg 0.6221 vs AVX asm avg 0.4967 and rep movsb avg 0.4970 (about 1.25x).
compiler_and_flags: cc (gcc per README) with -Wall -ggdb3 -fPIC -fpic -O3 for the C side; nasm -felf64 for the assembly; compiler version not stated
hardware: AMD A8-6410 APU (2 GHz) and Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY (2.5 GHz, cloud VM with hypervisor flag); CPU governor set to performance per README
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; AVX-512 variant needs AVX-512 (reported 'CPU is not supported' on the AMD A8); rep movsb performance depends on ERMS/FSRM support; routines are plain memcpy without small-size dispatch.
caveats: Author's own run, README makes no claim and result.txt has no units; glibc version and exact compiler version unknown; the harness is multithreaded (libs/memcpy_multithread.c), so it measures bandwidth-bound large copies more than small-size latency; gain over libc is only about 25 percent and AVX-512 is slower than AVX-256 on the Xeon. Tier A given because code, flags and CPU models are public, but a verifier may lower it for the missing compiler version and units.
found_via: github.com/topics/memcpy page, then repo README, result.txt and Makefile via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: CRYPTOGAMS (dot-asm/cryptogams perlasm kernels)
language: Perl-generated assembly (ARM, x86_64, PowerPC, s390x, RISC-V and others)
baseline: gcc-compiled C for the same algorithm (gcc-4.4 for ARM Poly1305, gcc 3.4 for x86_64 SHA-1), as given in the header comment tables
workload: Poly1305 block function on ARM11, Cortex-A5/A8/A9/A15 and Snapdragon S4 (integer ALU assembly versus gcc-generated code, plus a NEON path); SHA-1 block function on Opteron and Xeon (EM64T).
claimed_speedup: poly1305-armv4.pl header, 'IALU/gcc-4.4' column: IALU assembly 7.78 / 6.35 / 6.25 / 5.10 / 3.85 / 5.70 cycles per byte with gcc-4.4 output '+100% / +130% / +115% / +95% / +85% / +100%' (ARM11xx, Cortex-A5, A8, A9, A15, Snapdragon S4), NEON 3.00 / 2.36 / 2.55 / 1.25 / 1.48 on A5 / A8 / A9 / A15 / S4. sha1-x86_64.pl header: gcc 3.4 '+45%' on Opteron and '+65%' on Xeon relative to the new 6.8 / 9.9 cycles per byte assembly.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-4.4 and gcc 3.4, flags not stated (ARM table notes the integer path is for -march=armv6)
hardware: ARM11xx (ARMv6), Cortex-A5, A8, A9, A15, Snapdragon S4; AMD Opteron and Intel Xeon (EM64T) for the SHA-1 table
stars_or_usage: 70 stars; the assembly originates from the OpenSSL project and carries Linux __KERNEL__ guards
tradeoffs: Perl scripts generate per-architecture assembly selected by a 'flavour' argument; NEON paths need NEON-capable cores; the repo is a distribution mirror and ignores pull requests.
caveats: Performance data is a comment table in each .pl file, first-party and without a harness or compiler flags; the compilers (gcc 3.4 and 4.4) are very old, so modern compilers may close part of the gap; the percentage column is relative to the assembly figure (interpretation: compiler output is that much slower). The repo README itself has no performance numbers. Many other files contain similar tables; only two headers were read.
found_via: github.com/topics/cryptography?l=assembly page; perlasm headers read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: rt_memcpy_cm (Cortex-M assembly memcpy for RT-Thread)
baseline: C library memcpy (Keil) and RT-Thread's rt_memcpy
workload: Copying 10,000 bytes 10,000 times in a Keil environment.
claimed_speedup: README: RT-Thread rt_memcpy 1261 ms; assembly version 883 ms (1.43x, derived); C library memcpy 906 ms (assembly about 2.5% faster, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Keil (MDK) environment; optimization level and flags not stated; README lists KEIL, GCC and IAR as supported toolchains
tradeoffs: ARM Cortex-M3/M4/M7 only; intended as a replacement for rt_memcpy inside RT-Thread; Keil/GCC/IAR syntax variants.
caveats: Gain over the toolchain's own memcpy is only about 2.5% and could be within noise; single microbenchmark with no chip, clock, optimization level or alignment stated; README is in Chinese; last commit 2022.
found_via: github.com/topics/memcpy page listing, then repo README

name: cespare/xxhash (Go amd64/arm64 assembly)
baseline: the same package built with the purego tag (Go compiler output for the same XXH64 function)
workload: XXH64 Sum64 over inputs from 4 bytes to 10 MB.
claimed_speedup: README, asm vs purego: 4 B 1.2 vs 1.3 GB/s (asm slower), 16 B 3.5 vs 2.9, 100 B 8.1 vs 6.9, 4 KB 16.7 vs 11.7, 10 MB 17.3 vs 12.0 GB/s (about 1.4x at large inputs, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.19.2; benchstat over `go test -tags purego -benchtime 500ms -count 15 -bench 'Sum64$'` versus the default build
tradeoffs: Assembly only on amd64 and arm64 (purego fallback elsewhere); XXH64 only, no XXH3.
caveats: Baseline is the package's own pure-Go code, not C xxHash. Assembly is slower for 4-byte inputs. The README asserts 'much faster than anything in the Go standard library' without figures. Numbers measured with Go 1.19.2 (2022); newer Go compilers may narrow the gap. The tier A assumes the repo benchmarks (Sum64 benchmark in the repo) are the code that produced the table.
found_via: Not from a paper search: Go assembly projects with a stdlib or pure-Go baseline, checked on github.com (README read) after the paper searches yielded few C/C++ artifacts

name: tmthrgd/go-hex (SSE/AVX assembly hex)
workload: Hex encode and decode of 14 or 15 bytes up to 128 MB buffers.
claimed_speedup: README Go benchmarks: Encode 1k 11572.80 MB/s vs encoding/hex 451.49 MB/s (about 25x, derived); Decode 1k 6093.43 vs 245.43 MB/s (about 25x); Encode 128M 4793.16 vs 457.13 MB/s; Decode 128M 5397.68 vs 143.72 MB/s.

name: AlphaDev sort3-sort8 assembly programs (libc++ branchless sort3/4/5)
language: Python (RL pseudo-code) / C++ test harness with x86-64 assembly sort programs
baseline: libc++ std::sort with its previous __sort3/__sort4/__sort5 helpers
workload: Sorting random uint32 and uint64 arrays of size 1 to 262144 in the libc++ benchmarks, on isolated Skylake, ARM and AMD machines.
claimed_speedup: LLVM commit 194d1965d2 (Differential Revision D118029) message: branchless sort3/sort4/sort5 'generated using Reinforcement Learning' achieve 'statistically significant improvement in sorting random integers on test cases from sort1 to sort262144 for uint32 and uint64'; the commit gives no percentages (full table on an external spreadsheet link). The Nature 2023 paper's figures were not opened.
hardware: Intel Skylake, AMD and ARM machines (models not stated in the commit)
stars_or_usage: 740 stars; repository archived (read-only) by the owner on 2024-08-22; the sort3/4/5 routines were integrated into LLVM libc++
tradeoffs: The repo holds the RL agent pseudo-code and a test file with the discovered assembly sorts (Sort3AlphaDev to Sort8AlphaDev, VarSort3 to VarSort5); assembly execution is not included; libc++ integration is a branchless C++ translation for integral types only, fixed sizes 3 to 5.
caveats: The repo README and the LLVM commit give no percentages; the Nature paper (peer review is the reason for tier B) was not reachable, and forum snippets quoting 'up to 70% for short sequences, about 1.7% for large' were not verified. Programs were discovered by RL, not hand-written. Whether the variable-length sorts were upstreamed is unverified.
found_via: WebSearch 'AlphaDev sort3 sort4 sort5 libc++ std::sort assembly faster ...'; repo page and the llvm-project commit page on github.com

name: SIMDMatrixAlgorithm
language: x86-64 NASM assembly with C and C++ drivers
baseline: scalar C and scalar C++ matrix multiply compiled with gcc -O3
claimed_speedup: README table: scalar C ~0.6 s (<1 GFLOP/s); scalar C++ ~1.3 s; NASM XMM (SSE, 2x unroll) ~0.29 s (~10 GFLOP/s); NASM YMM (AVX, 4x unroll) ~0.0098 s (~28 GFLOP/s), about 60x versus scalar C (derived); hybrid C+ASM and C++ +ASM ~0.010 to 0.020 s.
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX/FMA only; fixed unrolling; single-precision square matrices.
caveats: Gap above 50x, so tier capped at C: the baseline is a naive scalar triple loop that stays unvectorized and uncached despite -O3 -mavx -mfma, so the gap reflects missing blocking and vectorization in the baseline, not asm versus well-optimized compiler output. GFLOP/s and CPI columns have no methodology. README mentions AVX-512 gains of about 30x with no zmm build or data (and the Ryzen 5 5600X has no AVX-512).
found_via: WebSearch 'github README hand-written assembly implementation benchmark table versus portable C compiled with gcc -O3'

name: CvsAssemblyBenchmark
baseline: GCC 12.2.0 -O3 C matrix multiply (i-k-j loop order)
workload: Dense double-precision 200x200 matrix multiply C = A x B, 1,000 iterations, mean of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: README: C 3.043 s vs hand-written assembly 1.823 s (internal timer), 3.067 s vs 1.847 s wall clock; ~2.63 vs ~4.39 GFLOP/s; 1.66x. The repo description's '~150% faster' does not match the README ratio.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.2.0 -O3 (Makefile also -Wall -Wextra -fPIE -pie, no -march flag listed); GNU as 2.40; assembly uses vfmadd231pd on YMM, inner loop 2x unrolled
hardware: x86-64 with AVX2/FMA, CPU model not given
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2/FMA only; fixed 200x200 double-precision kernel.
caveats: CPU model unstated, so tier C. No -march/-mavx2/-mfma flag is listed for the C build, so GCC probably emitted SSE2 only against an AVX2/FMA assembly kernel: the 1.66x gap is partly an unfair-flags effect. Description's headline (~150%) is inconsistent with the README (66% faster). Single small kernel.
found_via: github.com/topics/performance?l=assembly page listing ('Assembly is ~150% faster than C code'), then README

name: ademakov/bzero (DIY SSE/AVX bzero)
baseline: libc memset (bzero_0 in the README tables)
workload: Zeroing buffers of 0 to 2048 bytes on a Xeon E5520 and an i7-4850HQ.
claimed_speedup: README tables (lower is better), Xeon E5520: memset vs hand-written SSE asm bzero_7: 8 B 155 vs 61, 32 B 63 vs 51, 256 B 127 vs 79, 1024 B 317 vs 261, 2048 B 664 vs 552. i7-4850HQ: SSE asm wins to 256 B (8 B 72 vs 33; 256 B 82 vs 51) but loses at 1024 B (149 vs 189) and 2048 B (241 vs 392) where libc uses AVX.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O2 per README; version not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon E5520 @ 2.27 GHz (no AVX) and Intel Core i7-4850HQ @ 2.30 GHz (AVX)
tradeoffs: SSE2 routines lose to AVX-capable libc memset on large buffers; x86-64 only; meant as experiments, not a library.
caveats: Honest mixed result: wins mainly at small and mid sizes and on the non-AVX Xeon; libc memset is faster for large buffers on the AVX laptop. The author says newer AVX variants beat memset at all sizes, but those numbers were not in the README sections read. Units, libc version and flags other than -O2 are unstated; data from 2019.

name: minio/md5-simd (AVX2/AVX512 multi-buffer MD5)
workload: Aggregated MD5 hashing of many concurrent streams on 4 vCPUs with block sizes from 32 KB to 8 MB.
claimed_speedup: README AVX512 vs crypto/md5: 32KB 2229.22 -> 11605.78 MB/s (5.21x), 128KB 7.23x, 1MB 2233.56 -> 16941.95 MB/s (7.59x), 8MB 2182.48 -> 17252.88 MB/s (7.91x); single-thread block function BenchmarkBlock16 8228.88 MB/s vs BenchmarkCryptoMd5 687.66 MB/s. Description: 'up to 8x for AVX512 and 4x for AVX2'.
hardware: AWS EC2 c5.xlarge, Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M @ 3.0 GHz
tradeoffs: Multi-buffer design: the speedup appears only when many independent streams are hashed concurrently through its server API; AVX2/AVX512 x86-64 only.
caveats: Baseline crypto/md5 is a single-stream hash that is itself assembly on amd64 (not compiler output; not verified from the page); the single-stream comparison is not equivalent to the multi-buffer parallel test; Go version unstated. Only the AVX512 table is given with numbers.
